entities.name: Sosigenes of Alexandria
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sosigenes of Alexandria, an eminent Ancient Greek astronomer and mathematician of the 1st century BCE, is primarily remembered for his pivotal consultation with Julius Caesar in 46 BCE, which laid the intellectual groundwork for the comprehensive reform of the Roman calendar. Although his exact birth and death dates remain elusive, with his death placed around 100 BCE, his influence radiates from the bustling intellectual hub of Alexandria, a city renowned for its Hellenistic scholarship. His expertise was sought to address the severe inaccuracies of the existing Roman Republican calendar, a system so riddled with intercalary confusion that it had drifted by months from the actual solar year, causing civic and religious festivals to fall out of season.

According to the detailed account in Pliny the Elder's *Natural History* (18.210–212), Sosigenes advised Caesar on the design of a new calendar based on a purely solar year of 365.25 days. This advice directly led to the establishment of the Julian calendar, which introduced the concept of a regular leap year every four years, adding one day to February. This fundamental change, implemented in 45 BCE, effectively synchronized the Roman calendar with the Earth’s revolution around the sun, an astronomical achievement that stabilized timekeeping across the vast Roman Republic and later Empire. The reform required an extraordinary 'Year of Confusion' in 46 BCE, extended to 445 days, to realign the calendar.
